desk.name: Acid-Base Reactions
desk.description: Select any 2 chemicals to explore acid-base chemistry — neutralizations, gas evolution, precipitates, fumes, and indicator colour changes.

reactions.name: Strong Acid + Strong Base Neutralisation

output.observation: No visible colour change. Solution becomes warm — the reaction is exothermic. Use a thermometer to observe temperature rise.

reactions.educational_note: Classic neutralization: acid + base -> salt + water. pH changes from acidic to 7 at the endpoint.

reactions.name: Two Strong Acids Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Both are strong acids and cannot react with each other.

reactions.educational_note: Acids do not react with other acids. They both release H+ ions — there is no driving force for a reaction.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids — they cannot neutralise each other.

reactions.educational_note: Mixing two acids just gives a more acidic mixture. No neutralization can occur without a base.

reactions.name: HCl + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Vigorous fizzing and bubbling. Colourless, odourless CO2 gas is produced.

reactions.educational_note: Acids react with carbonates to produce CO2 gas. Test the gas with limewater — it turns milky white, confirming CO2.

reactions.name: HCl + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: Rapid fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Faster reaction than with Na2CO3.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonates react with acids like carbonates but need only one H+ ion. Same CO2 limewater test applies.

reactions.name: HCl + Calcium Hydroxide Neutralisation

output.observation: Cloudy limewater turns clear as it is neutralised. Solution warms slightly.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater (Ca(OH)2) is a weak base. It takes twice the moles of HCl to neutralise it.

reactions.name: HCl + Ammonia -> White Fumes!

output.odor: sharp pungent — ammonia and acid combined
output.observation: Dense white fumes/smoke instantly appear where the two vapours meet in air. Very dramatic and visible!

reactions.educational_note: This reaction happens in the gas phase — no liquid mixing needed! It is used as a lab test to identify HCl and NH3 gas.

reactions.name: HCl + Phenolphthalein Indicator

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays completely colourless — confirming the solution is acidic.

reactions.educational_note: Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.2. No colour = acid or neutral.

reactions.name: HCl + Universal Indicator

output.observation: Solution turns bright RED — very strong acid at pH 1.

reactions.educational_note: Universal indicator shows exact pH by colour: red (pH 1) to violet (pH 14).

reactions.name: HCl + Litmus Indicator

output.observation: Litmus turns from purple to bright red — confirming an acid.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus is the simplest acid-base indicator. Red = acid, Blue = base.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids only react with bases, metals, or carbonates — not with each other.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + NaOH Neutralisation (Diprotic)

output.observation: Solution becomes very hot — highly exothermic. No gas or precipitate. Temperature spikes noticeably.

reactions.educational_note: H2SO4 is diprotic — needs TWICE the moles of NaOH to neutralise compared to HCl. Key for titration calculations.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + NaOH Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild heat released. Faint soapy odour from sodium acetate. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acid + strong base gives a basic salt. The endpoint pH is above 7 because sodium acetate is slightly alkaline.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both chemicals are basic.

reactions.educational_note: Bases only react with acids — not with other bases.

reactions.name: NaOH + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: No visible change. Bicarbonate is converted to carbonate by the strong base.

reactions.educational_note: A strong base converts bicarbonate to carbonate. Useful concept in buffer chemistry.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: Bases require an acid to react. Two bases simply mix without reacting.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Ammonia smell from NH3 solution. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: No acid-base reaction possible between two bases.

reactions.name: NaOH + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Solution instantly turns bright pink/magenta — confirming a strongly basic environment.

reactions.educational_note: Phenolphthalein turns pink above pH 8.2. The stronger the base, the more vivid the pink.

reactions.name: NaOH + Universal Indicator -> Violet

output.observation: Solution turns deep violet/purple — very strong base at pH 14.

reactions.educational_note: Violet = pH 12-14 on universal indicator scale = strong alkali.

reactions.name: NaOH + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns from purple to blue — confirming a base/alkali.

reactions.educational_note: Blue litmus = base. The most fundamental acid-base test.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + NaOH Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild heat released. Citrus smell fades as the acid is neutralised.

reactions.educational_note: Citric acid is triprotic — needs 3 moles of NaOH to fully neutralise 1 mole of citric acid.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids cannot react with each other in a neutralization.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Very vigorous fizzing with CO2 gas. Solution also warms due to the strong acid.

reactions.educational_note: Strong acid + carbonate reacts more vigorously than weak acid + carbonate.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: Rapid and vigorous bubbling. CO2 produced quickly. Solution warms slightly.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonate reacts with H2SO4 releasing twice the CO2 per mole.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White milky precipitate of calcium sulfate forms immediately. Solution turns cloudy white. Heat also released.

reactions.educational_note: CaSO4 is insoluble in water — precipitates as a white solid. This is how gypsum is made industrially.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Ammonia Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild white mist near the surface. Ammonia smell disappears as it reacts. Solution warms. Produces ammonium sulfate (a fertiliser).

reactions.educational_note: Ammonium sulfate is a widely used fertiliser — industrially produced by exactly this reaction.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays completely colourless — confirming an acidic environment.

reactions.educational_note: Colourless result = pH below 8.2 = acidic or neutral.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Universal Indicator -> Red

output.observation: Solution turns deep red — pH 1, strongly acidic.

reactions.educational_note: Both HCl and H2SO4 show the same red at equimolar concentrations — universal indicator cannot tell them apart.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming an acidic solution.

reactions.educational_note: All acids turn litmus red. Litmus confirms acidity but not acid strength.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Moderate fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Vinegar smell present. Less vigorous than with strong acids.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acids react with carbonates more slowly than strong acids. CO2 limewater test still works.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Baking Soda — Classic Volcano!

output.observation: Vigorous foam and fizzing — the classic volcano reaction! Large bubbles and overflow if the container is small.

reactions.educational_note: The most famous safe acid-base reaction! Used in school volcanoes and science fairs worldwide.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Calcium Hydroxide

output.observation: Cloudy limewater becomes clear as it is neutralised. Mild heat released. Vinegar smell fades.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium acetate (product) is soluble — no precipitate forms. Solution clears as neutralisation occurs.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Ammonia

output.odor: mixed vinegar and ammonia, both fade
output.observation: Both vinegar and ammonia smells cancel out as neutralisation occurs. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acid + weak base = ammonium acetate. The solution is almost perfectly neutral (pH ~7). A rare balanced neutralisation.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays colourless — confirming an acidic solution even though it is a weak acid.

reactions.educational_note: Even weak acids keep phenolphthalein colourless as long as pH stays below 8.2.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Universal Indicator -> Orange

output.observation: Solution turns orange — weak acid at pH 3. Noticeably lighter than the red of HCl or H2SO4.

reactions.educational_note: Orange (pH 3) vs Red (pH 1): universal indicator CAN distinguish weak acids from strong acids — litmus cannot!

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming the solution is acidic. Vinegar smell present.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus turns red for ALL acids, weak or strong. It cannot distinguish between them.

reactions.name: Two Weak Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are weak acids. Smells like salad dressing!

reactions.educational_note: Even two different acids do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Two Base Salts Mixed

output.observation: No visible reaction. Both chemicals are basic sodium salts.

reactions.educational_note: Both are alkaline sodium salts and do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White milky precipitate of calcium carbonate (chalk) forms instantly. Solution turns cloudy white and settles over time.

reactions.educational_note: Double displacement reaction. CaCO3 (limestone/chalk) is insoluble and precipitates. NaOH stays in solution.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are basic.

reactions.educational_note: Bases cannot react in a neutralization without an acid present.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Turns pink — confirming that sodium carbonate solution is basic (alkaline).

reactions.educational_note: Na2CO3 is a base salt — its solution is alkaline due to hydrolysis. Phenolphthalein confirms this.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue — moderately strong base at pH 11.

reactions.educational_note: pH 11 = blue. Compare to NaOH (violet, pH 14) — you can see Na2CO3 is a weaker base.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming sodium carbonate solution is basic.

reactions.educational_note: Even base salts like Na2CO3 turn litmus blue — their solutions are alkaline.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Steady fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Citrus smell present. Moderate intensity.

reactions.educational_note: Same reaction used in bath bombs and effervescent drinks. Citric acid + carbonate = CO2 fizz.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White precipitate of CaCO3 forms. Solution becomes cloudy/milky white.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonate reacts with Ca(OH)2 to form insoluble CaCO3 — same principle used in water softening.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are weak bases.

reactions.educational_note: Two bases will not neutralise each other.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Phenolphthalein -> Very Faint Pink
reactions.formula: NaHCO3 (pH 8.3) -> Phenolphthalein turns VERY FAINT PINK

output.observation: A barely visible faint pink — NaHCO3 is only mildly basic (pH 8.3), just above the indicator threshold of 8.2.

reactions.educational_note: Faint pink distinguishes NaHCO3 from stronger bases like NaOH (deep pink). Great for comparing base strengths.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Universal Indicator -> Teal

output.observation: Solution turns teal/blue-green — mildly basic at pH 8. Much lighter than NaOH (violet) or Na2CO3 (blue).

reactions.educational_note: NaHCO3 is the mildest base in this set — perfect for comparing base strengths visually across all 4 bases.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Litmus -> Faint Blue
reactions.formula: NaHCO3 (weak base) -> Litmus turns FAINT BLUE

output.observation: Litmus turns to a faint light blue — NaHCO3 is mildly basic.

reactions.educational_note: Faint blue vs deep blue of NaOH shows baking soda is a very weak base — a great visual comparison.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Baking Soda — Effervescent Tablet!

output.observation: Gentle sustained fizzing with citrus smell — exactly like an Alka-Seltzer tablet dissolving in water.

reactions.educational_note: This is the exact reaction in effervescent tablets (Alka-Seltzer, vitamin C tablets). CO2 bubbles create the fizz.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: Two bases cannot neutralise each other.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Pink colour forms — Ca(OH)2 is basic. Slightly less vivid than NaOH as it is a weaker base.

reactions.educational_note: Ca(OH)2 is moderately strong base. Its pink is less vivid than NaOH — demonstrates base strength differences.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue — pH 12. Darker than Na2CO3 (pH 11) but lighter than NaOH (pH 14).

reactions.educational_note: Comparing Ca(OH)2, Na2CO3, and NaOH side by side shows a clear blue to violet progression.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming limewater is basic/alkaline.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater turning litmus blue is a classic school test.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Calcium Hydroxide

output.observation: Cloudy limewater becomes clear as it is neutralised. Mild heat produced. Citrus smell fades.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium citrate is the product — used as a calcium dietary supplement and food additive.

reactions.name: NH3 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Turns pink — confirming NH3 solution is basic. Ammonia smell present.

reactions.educational_note: NH3 is a weak base but pH is high enough to activate phenolphthalein. Compare its shade with NaOH.

reactions.name: NH3 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue at pH 11. Same shade as Na2CO3 — both are moderate bases at similar pH.

reactions.educational_note: NH3 and Na2CO3 both show pH ~11. Universal indicator cannot distinguish them by colour alone.

reactions.name: NH3 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming ammonia solution is a base.

reactions.educational_note: Even a weak base like NH3 turns litmus blue. Litmus confirms alkalinity but not strength.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Ammonia Neutralisation

output.odor: mixed citrus and ammonia, both fading
output.observation: Both citrus and ammonia smells gradually fade as they neutralise each other. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Ammonium citrate is produced — a weak acid + weak base salt. Used in food industry as an emulsifier.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Indicators are dyes — they only respond to acids or bases, not to each other.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators react with H+ or OH- ions, not with each other.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No reaction between two indicators.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators only respond to pH changes — not to other indicators.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays colourless — confirming citric acid is acidic.

reactions.educational_note: All acids keep phenolphthalein colourless. This test alone confirms something is an acid.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No reaction between two indicators.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators need acids or bases to show their colours — not other indicators.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Universal Indicator -> Red-Orange

output.observation: Solution turns red-orange — pH 2. Stronger than acetic acid (orange) but weaker than HCl (red).

reactions.educational_note: Citric acid at pH 2 sits between strong acids (pH 1) and acetic acid (pH 3). Universal indicator shows this beautifully.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming citric acid is an acid. Citrus smell present.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus confirms acidity of citric acid — same red as HCl and H2SO4. Cannot distinguish acid strength.
